title: Thermal Transformations and Mechanical Properties of All -d-metal  Mn 2 FeCu Heusler-Type Shape Memory Alloy
abstract: Abstract All-d-metal Heusler alloys are emerging functional materials in which magnetic ordering, lattice distortion, and mechanical behavior are strongly coupled through d–d electronic interactions. This study systematically investigates the structural, thermal, magnetic, and mechanical properties of Mn₂FeCu synthesized within a Heusler-type compositional framework. SEM/EDS revealed a dual-phase FCC-based microstructure consisting of Mn–Fe–rich and Mn–Cu–rich domains, while XRD confirmed FCC symmetry with compositional partitioning rather than full L2₁ ordering. Differential scanning calorimetry identified partial melting of the Cu-rich phase near ~ 900 °C. Dilatometry showed a thermoelastic FCC → FCT transformation at ~ 770–780 °C with a recoverable strain of ~ 0.067%. Magnetic thermogravimetric analysis determined a Néel temperature of 485 °C, indicating strong antiferromagnetic ordering and magneto-elastic coupling. Mechanical properties were highly processing-dependent. The as-cast condition exhibited the best strength–ductility balance (YS = 434 MPa, UTS = 632 MPa, 51% elongation), the quenched state maximized ductility (67%), and the furnace-cooled condition increased hardness (210.8 HV) but reduced elongation (20%). Fractography revealed transgranular ductile fracture in the as-cast and quenched states and intergranular fracture in the furnace-cooled condition. These findings demonstrate tunable thermo-magneto-structural behavior in Mn₂FeCu and highlight phase stability challenges in all-d Heusler alloys.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Shape memory alloys (SMAs) have attracted sustained scientific and technological interest for more than five decades owing to their ability to recover large, reversible strains through diffusionless martensitic transformations. Conventional systems such as Nickel–Titanium (NiTi), Copper-based alloys, and Iron-based alloys have been extensively investigated since the 1970s and have enabled numerous applications in actuators, biomedical devices, and adaptive structures [ 1 ,  2 ,  3 – 4 ]. Despite their widespread implementation, a persistent limitation remains: the relatively large thermal hysteresis associated with the first-order martensitic transformation (MT) and concerns regarding long-term microstructural stability under cyclic thermal or mechanical loading. These constraints hinder their deployment in high-precision, temperature-sensitive driving components where narrow transformation intervals and reproducible actuation are critical.

A significant conceptual and technological advance emerged with the discovery of the two-way shape memory effect (TWSME) accompanied by exceptionally low thermal hysteresis (< 1 K) in antiferromagnetic γ-Mn-based alloys, as first reported by Nosova and Vintaikin [ 5 ,  6 ]. This breakthrough demonstrated that Mn-rich systems could exhibit highly reversible thermoelastic martensitic transformations with minimal dissipative losses, thereby expanding the design space for temperature-controlled actuation. Subsequent investigations of Mn-rich Mn–Fe(Cu) alloys have revealed a rich interplay between structural, magnetic, and mechanical phenomena, including high damping capacity [ 7 ,  8 ], antiferromagnetic transitions [ 9 ,  10 ], and diffusionless FCC → FCT martensitic transformations [ 11 ]. More recently, Zhang et al. reported a magnetic shape memory effect in polycrystalline Mn–Fe–Cu alloys [ 12 ] and further clarified the relationship between the antiferromagnetic transition and the FCC–FCT martensitic transformation [ 13 ]. These studies collectively underscore the intrinsic interdependence between magnetic ordering and lattice instability in Mn-based alloys.

In Mn-based systems, the shape memory response and mechanical behavior are fundamentally governed by solid-state phase transformations, which can manifest through diverse crystallographic pathways depending on composition and thermal history [ 14 ,  15 ,  16 ,  17 ,  18 ,  19 – 20 ]. Rapid cooling from elevated temperatures can promote antiferromagnetic ordering below the Néel temperature ( T N ), a second-order paramagnetic–antiferromagnetic transition determined primarily by alloy chemistry. The coexistence or coupling of this magnetic transition with a first-order martensitic transformation provides a unique opportunity to tailor functional properties through compositional engineering and magneto-structural coupling.

Heusler alloys exhibiting the shape memory effect (SME) represent a distinct class of functional materials capable of reversible deformation under thermal, magnetic, or mechanical stimuli [ 1 ]. In magnetic shape memory alloys (MSMAs), magnetic-field-induced strain is particularly attractive because it avoids thermal inefficiencies and enables actuation frequencies at least three orders of magnitude higher than conventional thermally driven SMAs [ 2 ]. The diffusionless, first-order martensitic transformation in these materials gives rise to twin-variant rearrangement under external fields, producing large reversible strains with relatively small hysteresis [ 3 ,  4 ]. However, despite their promising multifunctionality, both magnetic and metamagnetic Heusler alloys suffer from intrinsic brittleness and low fracture toughness, which limit their structural reliability and technological implementation [ 21 ]. Attempts to enhance mechanical performance through compositional tuning, atomic disorder, and dopant incorporation have achieved only partial success in conventional  p–d  element Heusler systems [ 21 ].

The emergence of all -d- element Heusler alloys—first identified by Wei et al. as Heusler phases forming without  p- group elements [ 22 ]—has opened a promising research direction. First-principles calculations suggest that such systems, exemplified by stoichiometric Ni 2 MnTi, may exhibit superior mechanical properties compared to classical Heusler alloys [ 23 ] while retaining favorable magneto-structural coupling. Nevertheless, experimental investigations of the thermal stability, magneto-structural transformations, and mechanical behavior of ternary all -d- element Heusler compositions remain limited. In particular, although the Mn–Fe–Cu system has been examined in Mn-rich compositions for its damping capacity, antiferromagnetic transition, and martensitic behavior [ 7 ,  8 ,  9 ,  10 ,  11 ,  12 – 13 ], it has not been systematically evaluated in a strict Heusler configuration.

The primary purpose of this work is to establish, for the first time, a comprehensive thermal, magnetic, and mechanical characterization of an Mn–Fe–Cu ternary alloy engineered to satisfy the Heusler compositional framework. To the best of our knowledge, no prior study has investigated the Mn–Fe–Cu system in a true Heusler configuration while simultaneously examining its martensitic transformation, antiferromagnetic transition behavior, and mechanical performance.

The novelty of this research lies in (i) introducing the Mn–Fe–Cu system into the Heusler compositional regime, (ii) experimentally elucidating its coupled magneto-structural transformations, and (iii) delivering an integrated thermal–magnetic–mechanical assessment that bridges functional performance and structural reliability. By combining transformation thermodynamics with mechanical characterization, this study provides foundational data necessary for evaluating the viability of Mn–Fe–Cu Heusler alloys as next-generation low-hysteresis, magnetically responsive functional materials.

sections.heading: Materials and Methodology
paragraphs: A polycrystalline Mn–Fe–Cu alloy button ingot with a nominal mass of approximately 80 g was synthesized by arc-melting high-purity elemental constituents, Mn (99.99%), Fe (99.99%), and Cu (99.9%), on a water-cooled copper hearth under a high-purity argon atmosphere. Prior to melting, the arc-melting chamber was evacuated and purged repeatedly with argon to minimize oxygen and nitrogen contamination. Because manganese exhibits a high vapor pressure at elevated temperatures, a 5 at.% excess Mn was deliberately added relative to the target stoichiometry (Mn 50 Fe 25 Cu 25 ) to compensate for evaporative losses during melting. Each ingot was re-melted and inverted at least three times to promote chemical homogeneity and reduce segregation. The total mass loss after melting was limited to approximately 0.5%, indicating effective control of volatilization. The density of the consolidated ingot, determined using the Archimedes’ principle, was 7.50 g·cm⁻ 3 , confirming good densification and negligible porosity. Quantitative compositional analysis was performed using inductively coupled plasma–atomic emission spectrometry (ICP–AES), yielding a final composition of Mn 51.5 Fe 24.5 Cu 24  (at%), in close agreement with the intended Heusler-type composition and confirming that Mn compensation effectively mitigated volatilization effects.

For microstructural characterization, specimens were mounted in conductive bakelite and subjected to sequential grinding using SiC abrasive papers of progressively finer grit, followed by polishing with diamond suspensions to achieve a mirror-like surface finish. Care was taken to eliminate residual deformation layers and surface artifacts. The polished samples were examined using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) to assess grain morphology, phase distribution, and possible compositional inhomogeneities. Crystallographic phase identification was carried out using X-ray diffraction (XRD) on a PANalytical X’Pert Pro diffractometer equipped with CuKα radiation ( λ  = 1.5406 Å). Diffraction patterns were collected at room temperature over the angular range 20° ≤ 2θ ≤ 100°, enabling determination of phase constitution, lattice parameters, and potential long-range ordering consistent with a Heusler structure.

Thermal stability and transformation behavior were investigated using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), quenching dilatometry, and thermogravimetric analysis (TGA). DSC measurements were performed on cylindrical specimens (3 mm in diameter and 5 mm in length) placed in alumina crucibles and analyzed using a Netzsch STA 449 F5 Jupiter simultaneous thermal analyzer. Experiments were conducted under flowing argon from room temperature to 1250 °C at a constant heating rate of 10 °C·min⁻ 1 . These measurements enabled identification of melting temperatures, solid-state transformation temperatures, and associated enthalpic changes. Dimensional changes associated with thermal and martensitic transformations were examined by quenching dilatometry in accordance with ASTM E228-22. Specimens instrumented with a K-type thermocouple were positioned between alumina push rods in a Linseis R.I.T.A. L78 horizontal push-rod dilatometer. Heating was performed by induction from room temperature to 800 at 3 °C·min⁻ 1 , followed by an isothermal hold of 20 min to ensure thermal equilibration. Controlled cooling was subsequently carried out at 3 °C·min⁻ 1  under  an argon atmosphere while continuously recording linear dimensional changes. Thermogravimetric analysis under an applied magnetic field was conducted on specimens of identical geometry (3 mm × 5 mm) in alumina crucibles from room temperature to 1000 °C at a heating rate of 10 °C·min⁻ 1  in order to assess mass stability and potential magneto-structural coupling effects.

Mechanical properties were evaluated through hardness and uniaxial tensile testing to establish correlations between phase constitution, microstructure, and structural integrity. Vickers microhardness measurements were performed on polished bulk samples using a Struers Duramin-5 hardness tester equipped with a diamond indenter. A load of 4.91 N was applied for a dwell time of 5 s, and multiple indentations were taken to ensure statistical reliability. Uniaxial tensile testing was conducted on miniature MT2 specimens [ 24 ] with a thickness of 1 mm and a cross-sectional area of 1 mm 2  on a MiniTensile™ automated testing system (Product Innovation and Engineering), fabricated using wire electrical discharge machining to ensure dimensional precision and minimal residual stress. Prior to testing, specimen dimensions were measured at three locations along the gauge length and across the thickness using a micrometer screw gauge and averaged to minimize geometric uncertainty. Tensile tests were performed at room temperature under displacement control at a constant strain rate of 0.0033 s⁻ 1 , and a nominal pretension stress of 15 MPa was applied prior to testing to ensure proper alignment. Digital Image Correlation (DIC) was used to process the machine data using the proprietary software GOM correlate Professional 2020. The resulting stress–strain data were used to determine yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and ductility, thereby providing a comprehensive assessment of the mechanical performance of the Mn–Fe–Cu Heusler-type alloy.

sections.heading: Microstructure and Crystal Structure
paragraphs: Figure  1  presents the backscattered electron (BSE) micrograph of the Mn₂FeCu alloy together with the corresponding EDS elemental distribution maps. The BSE image reveals a distinctly heterogeneous microstructure consisting of two compositionally differentiated phases. In backscattered mode, contrast is governed primarily by atomic number (Z-contrast), such that regions enriched in higher atomic number elements appear brighter. The lighter gray phase therefore corresponds to Cu-enriched regions, whereas the darker phase is comparatively Fe-rich. Fig. 1 SEM BSE micrograph of Mn 2 FeCu with EDS mapping showing the elemental distribution. The light gray phase is Cu–Mn rich, and the darker gray phase is Fe–Mn rich both with FCC crystal structures

The EDS elemental maps substantiate this interpretation. Copper is strongly localized within the lighter regions, while iron segregates preferentially to the darker phase. Manganese is distributed across both regions, though with measurable partitioning between them. These observations confirm the presence of two chemically distinct phases: an Mn–Cu-rich phase and an Mn–Fe-rich phase. The morphology—characterized by interconnected domains on the order of several micrometers—suggests solidification-driven microsegregation and incomplete chemical homogenization in the as-cast condition.

Crucially, both phases exhibit crystallographic characteristics consistent with cubic symmetry, as verified by X-ray diffraction (Fig.  2 ). The presence of two chemically partitioned cubic phases indicates that the nominal Mn 2 FeCu composition does not stabilize as a single homogeneous phase under the present processing conditions. Instead, the system decomposes into two FCC-based solid solutions with slightly different lattice parameters arising from compositional variation. This behavior reflects the delicate balance between chemical ordering and phase separation in Mn-rich ternary systems. Fig. 2 X-ray Diffraction (XRD) patterns of  a  as-cast and  b  quenched Mn 2 FeCu alloy taken at room temperature

The X-ray diffraction patterns shown in Fig.  2 (a) and (b) for the as-cast and quenched Mn 2 FeCu alloy display characteristic reflections in the angular ranges 2θ ≈ 41–44°, 48–50°, and 70–73°, corresponding to the (111), (200), and (220) planes of a face-centered cubic (FCC) lattice. The presence of these reflections confirms that both compositional domains adopt an FCC-type structure.

The occurrence of closely spaced or broadened peaks in these regions indicates the coexistence of two FCC phases with slightly different lattice parameters, consistent with the Mn–Fe-rich and Mn–Cu-rich regions observed in SEM/EDS. Subtle lattice parameter differences arise from atomic size mismatch and differences in electronic interactions between Mn–Fe and Mn–Cu atomic pairs. The retention of FCC symmetry after quenching suggests that no martensitic transformation occurs within the investigated temperature range, or that the martensitic start temperature ( M S ) lies below room temperature.

According to the Open Quantum Materials Database (OQMD) [ 25 ,  26 ], Mn 2 FeCu is predicted to crystallize as a full magnetic Heusler alloy in the L2₁ structure with space group Fm3̅m (No. 225) and a lattice parameter of approximately 5.658 Å. The L2 1  structure represents an ordered derivative of the FCC lattice in which atomic species occupy well-defined sublattices, producing characteristic superlattice reflections. However, the experimental diffraction patterns predominantly exhibit fundamental FCC reflections, and the absence or weakness of distinct superlattice peaks suggests either incomplete long-range atomic ordering or partial decomposition into chemically distinct FCC phases.

The observed two-phase FCC microstructure in Mn₂FeCu highlights one of the emerging anomalies associated with all -d- metal Heusler alloys. Unlike conventional  p–d  Heusler systems—where main-group elements promote directional bonding and stabilize long-range L2 1  ordering— all -d  Heusler alloys rely exclusively on transition metal bonding interactions. The absence of  p- block elements modifies electronic hybridization, alters exchange interactions, and can reduce the thermodynamic driving force for strict atomic ordering. As a result, chemical partitioning, site disorder, and multiphase stabilization are frequently encountered.

These behaviors reflect the fact that all -d  Heusler alloys constitute a relatively new class of materials whose fundamental thermodynamic and kinetic characteristics are not yet fully understood. While computational databases such as OQMD predict stable L2 1  ordering for Mn₂FeCu, experimental realization may be complicated by competing solid-solution equilibria, sluggish ordering kinetics, or spin-dependent interactions that alter phase stability. In particular, the strong magnetic exchange between Mn and Fe can stabilize a Mn–Fe-rich  γ -phase, whereas the weaker magnetic interaction of Cu with Mn promotes segregation into a distinct Mn–Cu-rich FCC phase. The competition between magnetic stabilization and chemical ordering may therefore impede formation of a single-phase L2 1  structure.

Such deviations from ideal Heusler ordering should not be interpreted solely as processing deficiencies; rather, they underscore the complex interplay between electronic structure, magnetism, and chemical thermodynamics in all -d  systems. These intrinsic complexities distinguish all -d  Heusler alloys from classical Heusler compounds and partially explain the anomalous phase behavior frequently reported in this emerging materials class.

The coexistence of Mn–Fe-rich and Mn–Cu-rich FCC phases has important implications for the magnetic and functional behavior of Mn 2 FeCu. In Mn-based alloys, magnetic ordering and potential martensitic transformations are highly sensitive to local composition and lattice parameter. Compositional partitioning can modify exchange interactions, shift the Néel temperature, and influence magneto-structural coupling. Furthermore, incomplete L2 1  ordering may suppress the uniform magnetic moments predicted for a fully ordered Heusler phase, thereby altering the alloy’s transformation and magnetic response.

Overall, the combined microstructural and diffraction analyses demonstrate that although Mn₂FeCu is theoretically predicted to adopt a full L2 1  Heusler structure, the experimentally synthesized alloy stabilizes as a dual-phase FCC microstructure under the present conditions. This outcome exemplifies the evolving understanding of all -d- metal Heusler alloys, where theoretical predictions and experimental realities may diverge due to complex magnetic–chemical interactions. Continued investigation into heat treatment optimization, ordering kinetics, and magneto-structural coupling will be essential to fully elucidate the intrinsic behavior of this new generation of Heusler materials.

sections.heading: Thermal Phase Transformation
paragraphs: Figure  3 (a) and (b) presents the DSC thermograms of the Mn₂FeCu alloy in the as-cast and quenched conditions during continuous heating from room temperature to 1250 °C. In both thermal histories, two pronounced endothermic peaks are observed, indicating discrete thermal events associated with phase transformations. The first sharp endothermic reaction occurs at approximately 894 °C in the as-cast condition and shifts slightly to 905 °C in the quenched alloy. The second and more intense peak appears at ~ 1230 °C in both cases and corresponds to the complete melting of the alloy. Fig. 3 DSC thermograms of Mn 2 FeCu alloy in  a  as-cast and  b  quenched conditions showing transitions and melting point peaks

The higher-temperature peak at 1230 °C represents the bulk liquidus temperature and indicates that quenching does not significantly alter the equilibrium melting behavior. In contrast, the lower-temperature endothermic peak near 900 °C corresponds to the onset of partial melting. Previous investigations of Mn–Fe–Cu ternary systems have shown that above approximately 850 °C, the Cu-rich (Cu,  γ Mn) phase becomes thermodynamically unstable and begins to transform into a liquid phase, while the Fe-rich ( γ Fe,  γ Mn) phase remains solid [ 27 ]. The sharp peak observed in both thermograms therefore signifies the formation of a two-phase region consisting of liquid (Cu,  γ Mn) coexisting with solid ( γ Fe,  γ Mn). The small temperature shift between the as-cast and quenched conditions likely reflects subtle compositional redistribution or internal stress effects introduced during rapid cooling.

Beyond melting phenomena, Mn–Fe–Cu alloys are known to undergo solid-state structural transformations. It has been established that the ternary Mn–Fe–Cu system exhibits a martensitic transformation from an FCC parent phase to a face-centered tetragonal (FCT) structure [ 8 ,  28 ]. This diffusionless, first-order transformation is driven by lattice instability and magneto-elastic coupling. The tetragonal distortion arises from anisotropic elongation of the cubic lattice, lowering the free energy under specific compositional and magnetic conditions. Recent studies have further demonstrated that such structural distortions in Mn-rich systems are closely linked to magnetic ordering, producing complex thermo-magneto-structural responses at elevated temperatures [ 29 ].

The dilatometric response of the quenched Mn₂FeCu alloy is shown in Fig.  4 (a), with the derivative curves presented in Fig.  4 (b). During heating, a pronounced macroscopic expansion occurs at approximately 777 °C, clearly highlighted by the sharp peak in the derivative curve. This abrupt dimensional change is attributed to the FCC → FCT martensitic transformation. The tetragonal distortion involves elongation along one crystallographic axis relative to the parent FCC lattice, producing a measurable change in specimen length. The transformation temperature is consistent with the high-temperature martensitic behavior reported for Mn–Fe–Cu systems, which is strongly composition dependent [ 27 ]. Fig. 4 Dilatometric curves showing heating and cooling of quenched Mn 2 FeCu;  a  DL vs. temperature and  b  the derivative of ( a )

Notably, a symmetric large contraction is not observed during cooling. This asymmetry may be associated with atomic ordering or compositional rearrangement during the 20-min thermal hold at 800 °C. In all -d- metal Heusler-type systems, ordering kinetics and magnetic exchange interactions evolve significantly at elevated temperatures, potentially stabilizing one structural variant and suppressing or broadening the reverse transformation [ 23 ,  29 ]. Such behavior is increasingly recognized as characteristic of emerging all -d  Heusler alloys, where thermodynamic stability and transformation reversibility are still under active investigation [ 23 ].

Prior to the major expansion event, the derivative curves in Fig.  4 (b) reveal a forward transformation during heating between approximately 720 °C and 750 °C, and a corresponding reverse transformation during cooling between roughly 740 °C and 695 °C. These features indicate additional structural adjustments preceding the dominant FCC → FCT transition. Mn–Fe–Cu alloys are known to exhibit complex martensitic sequences involving multiple tetragonal variants [ 28 ]. Tsuchiya et al. [ 30 ,  31 ] reported that for Mn concentrations below about 60 at.%, spinodal decomposition can occur, leading to lattice distortion from FCC to modulated tetragonal phases (FCT 1  or FCT 2 ). The intermediate transformations observed here are consistent with such compositional and structural fluctuations, particularly in alloys approaching Heusler stoichiometry where site disorder and magnetic interactions further complicate phase stability.

The heating-induced expansion at ~ 777 °C corresponds to a recoverable strain of approximately 0.067%, while the recoverable strain upon cooling is about 0.0034%. Although modest compared to classical magnetic shape memory alloys, this reversible dimensional change confirms the thermoelastic nature of the martensitic transformation. As previously reported [ 6 ], Mn–Fe–Cu systems possess twin-structured martensite capable of twin boundary motion and variant reorientation, giving rise to recoverable strain during thermal cycling. Importantly, the alloy returns to its original dimension at the end of the heating–cooling cycle, demonstrating reversibility and the absence of permanent plastic deformation.

From a broader perspective, the complex sequence of partial melting, high-temperature FCC → FCT transformation, precursor distortions, and magnetically coupled dimensional changes exemplifies the anomalous transformation behavior increasingly reported in all -d- metal Heusler alloys. Unlike conventional  p–d  Heusler systems, the absence of  p- element-mediated bonding in all -d  alloys modifies electronic hybridization and magnetic exchange interactions, often resulting in multiphase stability, incomplete ordering, and coupled magneto-structural transitions. Because all -d  Heusler alloys constitute a relatively new class of functional materials, their intrinsic thermodynamic pathways and transformation mechanisms remain incompletely understood. The present thermal and dilatometric results therefore provide important experimental insight into the strongly coupled structural–magnetic behavior of Mn 2 FeCu and contribute to the growing understanding of phase stability in emerging all -d  Heusler systems.

sections.heading: Magnetic Transformation
paragraphs: Mn-rich Mn–Fe alloys are known to order antiferromagnetically below the Néel temperature ( T N ) when quenched from the high-temperature γ-phase, and this magnetic ordering is often accompanied by a subtle distortion of the parent FCC lattice due to magneto-elastic coupling [ 13 ]. In the present Mn₂FeCu alloy, the magnetic transformation corresponds to a paramagnetic-to-antiferromagnetic ordering transition. Figure  6  shows the magnetic thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) measurement performed on the quenched alloy to determine  T N . From the curve, the transformation onset occurs at approximately 444 °C and the endset at approximately 505 °C. The peak of the derivative curve, located at 485 °C, is defined as the Néel temperature of Mn₂FeCu. Below this temperature, the alloy is antiferromagnetically ordered, while above  T N  it exists in the paramagnetic state.

The relatively broad transformation interval (~ 60 °C) suggests magnetic heterogeneity, which is consistent with the compositional partitioning observed in the microstructural analysis. In Mn-based ternary systems, antiferromagnetic ordering is governed primarily by Mn–Mn exchange interactions, which are highly sensitive to interatomic spacing and electronic band filling. Substitutional elements such as Fe introduce competing exchange interactions, while Cu—being non-magnetic—modifies the electronic density of states and exchange pathways. Recent investigations of all -d- metal Heusler alloys have demonstrated that small compositional variations significantly influence magnetic ground states and ordering temperatures due to strong  d–d  hybridization effects [ 23 ,  29 ]. High-throughput computational studies further confirm that all-d Heusler systems exhibit highly tunable magnetic stability depending on site occupancy and electronic structure [ 32 ].

Zhang et al. [ 6 ] reported a Néel temperature of 463 K (~ 190 °C) for Mn 85.5 Fe 9.5 Cu 5.0 , where  T N  overlapped with the martensite start temperature ( M S ). The substantially higher  T N  observed in the present Mn₂FeCu alloy (485 °C) is attributed to compositional differences, particularly the increased Cu and Fe contents relative to Mn. Composition-dependent shifts in  T N  have been systematically reported in Mn-rich Heusler-related systems, where electronic structure modifications alter magnetic exchange energy [ 29 ]. The higher Cu fraction in Mn 2 FeCu likely stabilizes antiferromagnetic ordering at elevated temperatures through modification of Mn–Mn exchange interactions and local lattice distortion.

Previous studies [ 6 ,  12 ,  33 ] have consistently shown that in Mn-rich Mn–Fe(Cu) alloys, there is often an overlap or close proximity between  T N  and  M S . This coincidence has been attributed to strong magneto-structural coupling, where magnetic ordering alters the Gibbs free energy landscape of the parent and martensitic phases. Such coupling is now recognized as a defining feature of many all -d  Heusler systems. For example, recent work on NiCoMnTi-based all -d  Heusler alloys demonstrated that magnetic phase transitions can be systematically tuned through compositional engineering, directly influencing structural stability and transformation behavior [ 29 ]. Similarly, studies on Mn₂-based all -d  Heusler alloys have revealed strong correlations between magnetic order, tetragonal distortion, and structural phase stability [ 23 ].

Overall, the magnetic TGA results confirm that Mn₂FeCu undergoes a paramagnetic-to-antiferromagnetic transition at 485 °C, with a broad transformation window reflecting compositional and structural heterogeneity. The elevated Néel temperature relative to previously reported Mn-rich compositions [ 6 ] further highlights the strong compositional dependence of magnetic stability in Mn–Fe–Cu systems. These findings are consistent with recent advances in all-d Heusler research, which emphasize that magnetism, lattice distortion, and chemical ordering are strongly interdependent in this emerging class of functional materials [ 23 ,  29 ,  32 ]. The present results therefore contribute to the growing body of work demonstrating that magnetic ordering and martensitic transformations in all -d  Heusler alloys are inherently coupled phenomena requiring simultaneous thermodynamic and electronic consideration.

sections.heading: Mechanical Properties
paragraphs: Figure  7  presents the engineering stress–strain responses of Mn₂FeCu in three distinct conditions: as-cast, quenched from 1000 °C after 24 h, and furnace-cooled from 1000 °C after 60 h. The mechanical response demonstrates a pronounced sensitivity to thermal history, reflecting the strong dependence of strength and ductility on phase constitution, defect density, and microstructural evolution. Fig. 7 Stress–strain curves of Mn 2 FeCu in the as-cast, quenched, and furnace-cooled conditions showing the relationship between heat treatment and mechanical properties

The as-cast condition exhibits the highest strength among the three states, with a yield strength (YS) of 434 MPa and an ultimate tensile strength (UTS) of 632 MPa, while maintaining a substantial elongation to fracture of 51%. The high strength of the as-cast alloy is attributed to solidification-induced microsegregation and a refined two-phase microstructure, which likely promote strengthening through compositional partitioning and phase boundary reinforcement. The coexistence of Mn–Fe–rich and Mn–Cu–rich FCC domains may provide barriers to dislocation motion, thereby enhancing yield strength through a composite-like strengthening mechanism. Additionally, residual stresses introduced during solidification may contribute to the elevated yield response.

The quenched condition displays a markedly different mechanical profile. Although its YS (235 MPa) and UTS (445 MPa) are lower than those of the as-cast alloy, the elongation to fracture increases significantly to 67%, indicating enhanced ductility. Rapid quenching likely suppresses extensive grain growth and may retain a metastable solid solution with reduced segregation, thereby lowering strength but promoting uniform plastic deformation. The enhanced ductility may also reflect improved twin boundary mobility if a martensitic or tetragonally distorted phase is retained at room temperature, facilitating strain accommodation through twin reorientation mechanisms typical of Mn-based shape memory alloys.

In contrast, the furnace-cooled condition demonstrates the least favorable balance between strength and ductility. With a break strain of only 20%, YS of 329 MPa, and UTS of 467 MPa, this condition exhibits moderate strength but significantly reduced ductility. Prolonged exposure at 1000 °C for 60 h followed by slow cooling likely promotes grain coarsening, phase coarsening, and possibly enhanced chemical ordering. Larger grain sizes reduce the number of grain boundary barriers to dislocation motion, which ordinarily would lower yield strength according to the Hall–Petch relationship. However, coarse grains also concentrate strain incompatibilities at grain boundaries, promoting early crack initiation and reducing uniform elongation. Furthermore, extended high-temperature exposure may have led to incipient liquid formation in the Cu-rich phase, as suggested by the DSC results. Any transient liquid film penetration along grain boundaries could cause boundary weakening or localized compositional enrichment upon solidification, facilitating intergranular decohesion and thereby reducing ductility.

Despite these differences, all three conditions exhibit predominantly ductile fracture behavior, indicating that catastrophic brittle cleavage is suppressed in this alloy system. The absence of abrupt fracture suggests that the FCC-based matrix and multiphase microstructure retain sufficient plasticity for engineering applications.

Figure  8 (a) presents the Vickers hardness values of Mn₂FeCu under the three processing conditions. The furnace-cooled condition exhibits the highest hardness (210.8 HV), followed by the as-cast condition (198.8 HV), while the quenched condition displays the lowest hardness (152.9 HV). The furnace-cooled alloy is approximately 8.5% harder than the as-cast condition and 27.5% harder than the quenched condition, while the as-cast alloy is approximately 23.1% harder than the quenched alloy. Fig. 8 a  Vickers hardness of Mn 2 FeCu alloy in the as-cast, quenched, and furnace-cooled  b  thickness reduction by cold rolling of as-cast Mn 2 FeCu alloy after 10 passes through the roller

The higher hardness of the furnace-cooled alloy, despite probable grain coarsening, suggests that additional strengthening mechanisms are operative. One possible explanation is enhanced chemical ordering during prolonged heat treatment, leading to increased lattice friction stress and dislocation resistance. In all -d- metal Heusler-related alloys, ordering can significantly influence mechanical stiffness and hardness due to stronger directional  d–d  hybridization and modified bonding character [ 34 ,  35 ]. Additionally, if spinodal decomposition or phase partitioning occurred during slow cooling, the resulting compositional modulations may act as nanoscale obstacles to dislocation motion, increasing hardness even in the presence of larger grains [ 36 ]. The apparent deviation from classical Hall–Petch expectations may also indicate the onset of inverse Hall–Petch behavior in coarse-grained or ordered systems, where grain boundary-mediated deformation mechanisms become less dominant than lattice-controlled mechanisms [ 37 ].

The lower hardness in the quenched condition aligns with its enhanced ductility, consistent with reduced lattice resistance and lower dislocation density. Rapid cooling may suppress ordering and limit precipitation, thereby reducing strengthening contributions from second-phase particles or compositional modulations.

Figure  8 (b) demonstrates the cold rolling performance of the as-cast Mn 2 FeCu alloy, showing a thickness reduction of approximately 28.6% after ten passes without evidence of cracking or fracture. This substantial plastic deformation confirms that the alloy possesses sufficient workability for mechanical processing such as wire drawing. The ability to undergo significant thickness reduction without fracture is particularly promising for actuator or sensor applications, where wire or thin-strip geometries are often required. Further thickness reduction is likely achievable through intermediate annealing treatments to restore ductility via recrystallization and stress relaxation.

Overall, the mechanical data indicate that the as-cast condition provides the most favorable balance between strength and ductility, the quenched condition maximizes ductility at the expense of strength, and the furnace-cooled condition enhances hardness but reduces elongation. These results highlight the strong influence of thermal history on the microstructure–property relationship in Mn 2 FeCu and underscore the tunability of mechanical performance in this all -d  Heusler-related alloy system.

Figure  9  presents the backscattered electron (BSE) and secondary electron (SE) fractographs of the tensile fracture surfaces of Mn₂FeCu in the as-cast, quenched, and furnace-cooled conditions. The combined use of BSE and SE imaging provides complementary insight into both compositional contrast and surface topography, enabling detailed interpretation of the fracture mechanisms operative under each thermal condition. Fig. 9 Fractographs of the fracture surface of Mn 2 FeCu alloy in different conditions.  a ,  b , and  c  BSE images and  d ,  e , and  f  secondary electron (SE) images of as-cast, quenched and furnace-cooled, respectively

The as-cast condition (Fig.  9 (a) and (d)) exhibits clear features characteristic of ductile fracture. The fracture surface is dominated by uniformly distributed, micro-isometric dimples indicative of micro-void nucleation, growth, and coalescence—the classical mechanism of ductile failure in metallic systems. The dimples are relatively deep and equiaxed, suggesting significant plastic deformation prior to fracture. Additionally, visible shear lips and evidence of gliding along the fracture plane indicate substantial shear deformation and localized plastic flow. The reduction in cross-sectional area observed macroscopically during tensile testing correlates with the extensive stretching visible at the microscale. Crack propagation occurs predominantly across grains rather than along grain boundaries, confirming a transgranular ductile fracture mode. This behavior is consistent with the relatively high strength and good ductility measured in the as-cast condition, where phase boundaries and compositional heterogeneities act as obstacles to dislocation motion without promoting brittle interfacial decohesion.

The quenched condition (Fig.  9 (b) and (e)) similarly displays pronounced ductile features, but with even greater evidence of plastic flow. The dimple morphology appears more elongated in certain regions, reflecting enhanced plastic instability and greater uniform elongation prior to failure, in agreement with the 67% elongation recorded during tensile testing. The lower yield strength in this condition facilitates more homogeneous dislocation glide and void growth before final rupture. The fracture surface shows extensive tearing ridges and pronounced micro-void coalescence, again confirming a transgranular ductile fracture mechanism. The absence of cleavage facets or river patterns further supports the dominance of ductile failure. The improved ductility of the quenched condition is therefore directly reflected in the fractographic features, where greater plastic accommodation precedes crack propagation.

In contrast, the furnace-cooled condition (Fig.  9 (c) and (f)) exhibits a markedly different fracture morphology. Although some dimpling is still present, it is less pronounced and shallower compared to the as-cast and quenched states. The fracture surface reveals limited stretching and minimal reduction in area, consistent with the lower elongation (20%) measured mechanically. More significantly, crack propagation is observed to occur preferentially along grain boundaries, as evidenced by grain boundary outlines and separation planes visible in both BSE and SE images. This indicates that grain boundary cohesion is reduced relative to the grain interior.

The intergranular fracture mode in the furnace-cooled alloy likely arises from microstructural changes induced during prolonged heat treatment at 1000 °C followed by slow cooling. As suggested by the DSC analysis, partial melting of the Cu-rich phase occurs near 900 °C. Extended exposure at 1000 °C could therefore promote localized liquid formation and segregation along grain boundaries. Upon slow cooling, these segregated regions may solidify as compositionally distinct boundary films or precipitates, weakening intergranular cohesion. Such grain boundary embrittlement promotes crack initiation and propagation along boundaries rather than through grains, resulting in an intergranular ductile fracture mode. The presence of limited dimpling indicates that micro-void formation still occurs, but the preferential path of crack propagation shifts to grain boundaries due to localized weakening.

The transition from predominantly transgranular ductile fracture (as-cast and quenched) to intergranular ductile fracture (furnace-cooled) correlates directly with the mechanical data. The furnace-cooled condition exhibits higher hardness and elastic modulus but reduced ductility, reflecting increased lattice resistance and reduced grain boundary cohesion. In ordered or partially ordered intermetallic systems, enhanced ordering can increase hardness while simultaneously reducing grain boundary ductility, especially if segregation or secondary phase formation occurs at interfaces (Table  1 ). Overall, the fractographic evidence confirms that Mn₂FeCu retains ductile fracture characteristics in all conditions, but the dominant fracture path and degree of plastic deformation are strongly dependent on thermal history. The as-cast and quenched states fail via transgranular micro-void coalescence with significant plasticity, while the furnace-cooled state exhibits intergranular ductile fracture associated with grain boundary weakening. These observations reinforce the strong coupling between thermal processing, microstructural evolution, and mechanical performance in Mn₂FeCu, further highlighting the tunability of fracture behavior in this all-d Heusler-related alloy system.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: This study provides a comprehensive structural, thermal, magnetic, mechanical, and fractographic evaluation of Mn₂FeCu engineered within a Heusler-type compositional framework. The combined microstructural, diffraction, thermal, magnetic, and mechanical analyses collectively demonstrate that Mn₂FeCu exhibits strongly coupled thermo-magneto-structural behavior characteristic of emerging all-d-metal Heusler alloys.

Microstructural characterization revealed a dual-phase FCC-based constitution consisting of Mn–Fe–rich and Mn–Cu–rich domains, rather than a fully homogenized single L2₁ Heusler phase. XRD confirmed FCC symmetry with peak splitting indicative of compositional partitioning and incomplete long-range ordering. These findings highlight one of the intrinsic complexities of all-d Heusler systems: thermodynamic competition between ordered Heusler structures and phase-separated FCC solid solutions. The results contribute experimentally to the growing body of evidence that the realization of ideal L2₁ ordering in all-d systems is kinetically and thermodynamically non-trivial.

Thermal analysis identified two key transformations: (i) partial melting of the Cu-rich phase near ~ 900 °C and (ii) a high-temperature FCC → FCT martensitic transformation near ~ 770–780 °C. Dilatometry confirmed measurable recoverable strain (~ 0.067%), validating thermoelastic behavior. Magnetic thermogravimetric analysis determined a Néel temperature of 485 °C, significantly higher than values reported for more Mn-rich Mn–Fe–Cu systems, underscoring strong compositional sensitivity of magnetic ordering. The proximity and interaction between magnetic and structural transformations confirm pronounced magneto-elastic coupling in Mn₂FeCu, consistent with emerging understanding of all-d Heusler alloys where magnetic exchange and lattice distortion are energetically intertwined.

Mechanical testing revealed substantial tunability through thermal processing. The as-cast condition provided the most favorable balance of strength and ductility (YS = 434 MPa, UTS = 632 MPa, 51% elongation). The quenched state maximized ductility (67% elongation) at reduced strength, while the furnace-cooled condition increased hardness (210.8 HV) but reduced ductility (20%). Fractographic analysis demonstrated a transition from transgranular ductile fracture in the as-cast and quenched states to intergranular ductile fracture in the furnace-cooled state, likely due to grain boundary segregation and ordering effects. These findings confirm strong microstructure–property coupling and demonstrate that Mn₂FeCu retains significant plastic workability, as evidenced by successful cold rolling without cracking.
